title: Etodjey, Cassava-Leaf Sauce with Groundnuts
author: Milcos (via Karelle Vignon-Vullierme)
desc: 420 g of cassava leaves cooked down with 260 g of groundnut powder, a poached fish, dried fish and a nokoss — a Casamance sauce for rice.
longDesc: The cassava-leaf sauce of the Casamance, in a version by a friend of the site’s author, Milcos. A yaboye fish is poached about 20 minutes in lightly seasoned water and set aside. Chopped or pounded cassava leaves boil in a litre of water; squash goes in; five to seven minutes later a piece of dried fish; a quarter hour later the groundnut powder, the whole chile, the nokoss; and finally the flaked fish, simmered a final ten minutes. The sauce should reach a particular consistency and the water should evaporate slightly.
ingredients: 420 g cassava leaves, washed, then chopped or pounded
1 small chile (or a little chile powder)
3 garlic cloves, or more to taste
equipment: Mortar or blender for the nokoss
Smaller pot to poach the fish
steps: Poach the fish about 20 minutes in lightly salted, peppered water. Set it aside.
Boil water in a large pot, add the cassava leaves, and top up with water as needed. Add the squash.
After 5 to 7 minutes, add the dried fish and cook over medium-high heat.
About a quarter of an hour later, add the groundnut powder, then the whole chile.
Make the nokoss from the aromatics in the list (onion, green-onion stalks, parsley, garlic) — the extract does not itemise it — and add it. Cook 5 to 7 minutes.
Flake the poached fish, add it, lower the heat and simmer a further ten minutes or so.
The sauce is ready when it reaches the right consistency and the water has evaporated slightly. Serve with rice.
chefTips: The source’s three cues are ‘la sauce doit avoir cette consistance’, ‘l’eau doit s’évaporer légèrement’, and ‘c’est prêt’ — look for a thick, spoon-coating sauce.
The source’s yield is ‘pour environ 8/10 personnes’.
The poaching liquid for the fish can be used to top up the pot.
No Jola attribution is made on this page: it says only that the Casamance is a natural and historic region.
commonMistakes: Adding the groundnut powder too early and scorching.
Letting the water boil away before the fish goes in.
reheating: Gentle heat with a little water.
healthBenefits: Cassava leaves are rich in protein, vitamin C and iron.
culturalNote: Several au-senegal.com pages call étodié a traditional Diola dish and ‘le plat préféré des Diolas’. The page used here makes no ethnic attribution — it says only that the Casamance is ‘une région naturelle et historique du Sénégal’, so it is labelled by region.
sources: Source: lesgourmandisesdekarelle.com, ‘Etodjey (Etodié), sauce aux feuilles de manioc (Casamance, Sénégal)’. No article byline; the sidebar prints ‘Karelle Vignon-Vullierme’; the body credits the cook: ‘mon ami Milcos (qui a créé la marque Niofar)’. No date in the body (metadata 2018-09-17, modified 2020-01-15). Yield: ‘pour environ 8/10 personnes’. SINGLE-PASS.

ATTRIBUTION as the sources state it: this page names the Casamance only; two au-senegal.com pages call the dish ‘un plat traditionnel Diola’ (title of one: ‘L’étodié, le plat préféré des Diolas’, by Amédine Faye). No source names a place of origin. No Jola-language orthography is given by any source.

UNRECONCILED SECOND VERSION, not published: Amédine Faye’s au-senegal.com printing has essentially no quantities and puts the fish in ‘près de deux heures’ of simmering; this version has weights and about 50 minutes of pot time. The two simmering times disagree and neither is adopted.

Times printed: ‘une vingtaine de minutes’ (fish), ‘5/7 minutes’, ‘une quinzaine de minutes’, ‘5/7 minutes’ and ‘une dizaine’. Cues in short fragments: ‘La sauce doit avoir cette consistance’; ‘L’eau doit s’évaporer légèrement’; ‘C’est prêt !’.
The nokoss is named in the method but its contents are not itemised in the extract used here; the step reading above is an editorial grouping.
